area: Area VI. Flight by Reference to Instruments
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how a constant rate climb or descent differs from a constant airspeed one, teach the entry, the stabilized climb or descent, straight and turning, and both level-offs on round dials and glass, full panel and partial panel, explain the VSI's trend, rate and lag, connect the maneuver to approach descents, fly it from the right seat while explaining it, and analyze and correct the common errors an examiner simulates.
why: The ILS final is flown like a constant rate descent: from the outer marker to the middle marker the pilot adjusts pitch to hold the proper rate of descent and power to hold the proper airspeed, and the IFH calls that the heaviest demand on pilot technique [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]. Unless ATC says "at pilot's discretion" or adds a restriction, the AIM asks for climbs and descents of 500 to 1,500 fpm in the last 1,000 feet [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]], and on a nonprecision approach the pilot can find a target rate of descent from the vertical descent angle and the groundspeed [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]. It is also the maneuver that makes the VSI, with its lag, the primary pitch instrument [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]], and that needs coordinated pitch and power, where a change to one variable needs a coordinated change in the other [[23:209|IFH 7-48]].

chunks.title: What Task E asks, and how it differs from Task D

body.p: **Teaching constant rate climbs and descents** means teaching a student to hold a chosen vertical speed and a chosen airspeed at the same time [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. The sibling lesson FII.VI.D covers constant airspeed climbs and descents, FII.VI.A covers the two teaching methods, failure simulation and the positive exchange of controls, and FII.VI.B covers turns. This lesson builds on them and does not repeat them. The Instrument lesson IR.IV.A covers the pilot's side.

The difference from Task D is which control does which job. In a constant airspeed climb the power stays at the climb setting, the tachometer or manifold pressure gauge is the primary power instrument, and pitch holds the airspeed, so the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. In a constant rate climb, once the vertical speed needle stabilizes it becomes primary for pitch, and the airspeed indicator becomes primary for power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Descents split the same way: in a constant airspeed descent any airspeed deviation calls for a pitch adjustment, while in a constant rate descent the VSI is primary for pitch and the airspeed indicator for power [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: The VSI: trend, rate and lag

body.p: **Using the vertical speed indicator** well starts with how it works. The inside of its aneroid and the instrument case are both vented to the static system, but the case is vented through a calibrated orifice, so its pressure changes more slowly. In a climb that difference moves the pointer up; when the airplane levels off, the pressures equalize and the pointer returns to zero [[23:103|IFH 5-8]]. The pointer lags a few seconds behind the actual change, but the VSI is more sensitive than the altimeter [[23:103|IFH 5-8]].

It gives two kinds of information. Trend information is the immediate direction the needle moves; rate information is the stabilized rate. If the pitch is held constant, the needle settles after a short period, 6 to 9 seconds, and shows the rate; that delay is the lag [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]. The IFH says the same thing: the VSI is both a trend and a rate instrument [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

head: Fact
What to teach
Source
rows: Lag grows with the size and speed of the pitch change
A slow, smooth change gives minimum lag; a large, abrupt one gives erratic needle movement, a reverse indication and a longer delay
Rough control and turbulence
Both stretch the lag and make the rate erratic. In turbulence use the average of the swings, lean on the less sensitive altimeter, and do not chase the needle

The VSI shows a continuous zero and the altimeter freezes; on the alternate static source the VSI shows a momentary climb

body.p: Teach the overcontrolling test the IFH gives: when control pressure is applied and the VSI shows more than 200 fpm beyond the rate wanted, the pilot is overcontrolling. Aiming for 500 fpm, a reading over 700 fpm is too much [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

callout.text: Application: on the ground, show the student the needle at rest and have her say what she will use as zero. In the air, at a safe altitude, make one slow pitch change and one abrupt one and let her watch the difference in the needle [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

check.q: Your student moves from the school's round-dial trainer to a glass-panel airplane and says she will still wait 6 to 9 seconds for the VSI. What do you tell her?
check.a: The IFH says the glass VSI tape, fed by a digital air data computer, shows no lag [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. The airplane itself still takes time to settle at a new rate, so she should still hold the new attitude and be patient [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

chunks.title: Entering a constant rate climb, full panel

body.p: **Procedure using full panel for an entry into a constant rate climb.** The IFH builds it on the constant airspeed entry from climb speed, where the pilot first slows to climb speed in straight-and-level flight [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Then, as the power is increased to the approximate setting for the desired rate, raise the miniature aircraft at the same time to the climbing attitude for the desired airspeed and rate of climb [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

body.p: If the transition is smooth, the VSI shows an immediate upward trend, keeps moving slowly, and then stops at a rate that fits the stabilized airspeed and attitude [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. The IFH does not say why the airspeed indicator leads. A useful explanation (Application): changes do not produce instant, stabilized results, so the student must be patient while the new speed and vertical speed settle [[23:211|IFH 7-50]], and the airspeed indicator itself has very little lag [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]. It is still not instant: the airplane's momentum can delay what it shows, so it should not be the only pitch reference [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].

**On a glass panel** the entry is the same: as power is added, raise the yellow chevron to the pitch attitude that equates to the desired vertical speed. The airspeed tape is primary for pitch until the vertical speed stabilizes; then the VSI tape becomes primary for pitch and the airspeed tape primary for power. Small pitch changes fix any deviation from the desired vertical speed [[23:208|IFH 7-47]] [[23:209|IFH 7-48]].

Heading and trim are maintained as in straight-and-level flight [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. As power is increased the airplane tends to yaw and roll left unless aileron and rudder counter it [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]; in a climb, P-factor and torque add to that, so right rudder and aileron pressure are needed [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

callout.text: Climb entry: slow to climb speed, then power and pitch together. Airspeed for pitch until the needle settles; then VSI for pitch, airspeed for power.

check.q: On the entry to a 500 fpm climb your student stares at the VSI as it swings and keeps changing the pitch. What do you coach?
check.a: Until the vertical speed nears the target, the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch; the VSI takes over as its needle stabilizes [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Hold the new attitude and give it time to settle [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

chunks.title: The stabilized climb, straight and turning

body.p: **A stabilized constant rate straight climb or climbing turn, using the vertical speed indicator.** Straight: the VSI is primary for pitch, the airspeed indicator primary for power and the heading indicator primary for bank, with the attitude indicator supporting pitch and bank and the turn coordinator supporting bank [[23:176|IFH Figure 7-27]]. During climbs the VSI is used to change altitude at a desired rate, and pitch and power are adjusted to hold that rate [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].
Pitch and power corrections must be prompt and closely coordinated [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]; a change to any one variable needs a coordinated change in the other [[23:209|IFH 7-48]]:

Add power; as it comes in, lower the nose slightly to keep the rate

Lower the nose slightly, then watch the airspeed to see whether power is also needed

More pitch raises the rate for a moment, but the added drag soon costs airspeed unless power is added too

body.p: Knowing the approximate power settings keeps these corrections small [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. The rate a given pitch and power produce varies with weight and atmospheric conditions [[23:208|IFH 7-47]], and a normally aspirated engine loses power as altitude increases, so the pilot keeps advancing the throttle to hold the climb setting [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Application: in a long constant rate climb, expect to add power as you go to hold the airspeed.

**Climbing turns.** Combine the straight climb technique with the turn techniques, consider the aerodynamic factors affecting lift and power when choosing power settings, and speed up the cross-check to control bank as well as pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. As the bank increases the vertical lift component decreases, so check the altimeter, VSI and attitude indicator and raise the nose slightly; with the airspeed indicator primary for power, adjust the throttle as drag increases [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Set the approximate bank on the attitude indicator, then hold standard rate with the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft as the primary bank reference [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]; on a PFD the turn rate indicator is primary for bank in a standard rate turn [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. Steep banks significantly decrease the rate of climb, so keep the bank shallow and constant [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

callout.text: Application: at climb speed the standard rate bank is smaller than at cruise. By the IFH rule of thumb, 15 percent of true airspeed, 90 knots needs about 13.5° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Have the student say the bank before she rolls in.

check.q: In a 500 fpm climbing turn to the left, the VSI drops to 350 fpm and the airspeed sags as your student rolls in. What happened, and what is the fix?
check.a: The bank reduced the vertical lift and added drag. Raise the nose slightly for the rate and add power to hold the airspeed, since the airspeed indicator is primary for power [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:209|IFH 7-48]].

chunks.title: Partial panel: entries, climbs and descents without the gyros

body.p: **Procedure using partial panel.** Except the instrument takeoff, every IFH maneuver can be flown with the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]], and on glass with the AHRS simulated or inoperative [[23:194|IFH 7-33]]. The PTS requires Area VI to be taught both full panel and with backup or partial panel instruments [[FAA-S-8081-9E:17|PTS Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills]].

body.p: With limited instruments, only small, precise inputs: rapid control movements compound a deviation, set up an oscillation that can disorient the pilot, and fixation on the altimeter can cost heading and airspeed control [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

**Glass AHRS failure.** In the IFH example an AHRS failure removes all heading and attitude from the PFD and all autopilot modes except roll and altitude hold; the altimeter and the VSI tape are still shown [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. If the primary instrumentation on the PFD fails, the standby instruments are an analog airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and magnetic compass, with no standby turn coordinator [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Application: there is no standby VSI in that set either, so a rate on standby instruments has to be judged from how fast the altimeter moves, the way the IFH teaches pitch without an attitude indicator [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

callout.text: Application: brief on the ground when and how you will cover the gyros, and do it at a safe altitude. FII.VI.A covers how to set up failures safely.

check.q: With the attitude and heading indicators covered, your student tries to enter a 500 fpm climb straight from cruise and the airspeed swings 15 knots. What does the IFH suggest?
check.a: Partial panel climb entries are easier and more accurately controlled from climbing speed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]: slow to climb speed in level flight first, then add power for the rate and raise the nose, with small inputs [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

chunks.title: Leveling off from a constant rate climb

body.p: **A level-off from a constant rate straight climb or climbing turn** starts before the target altitude, because the airplane keeps climbing at a decreasing rate through the transition. Lead the altitude by 10 percent of the vertical speed: 50 feet at 500 fpm, 100 feet at 1,000 fpm [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] [[23:209|IFH 7-48]].

head: Level-off at
Technique
Source
rows: Cruise airspeed

Smooth, steady forward pressure toward the level attitude for the speed wanted. The VSI moves slowly to zero, the altimeter slows and the airspeed shows acceleration. Keep adjusting pitch and torque control as the speed builds, and reduce to cruise power before reaching cruise speed; the lead depends on how fast the airplane accelerates
Climbing airspeed

Lower the nose to the level attitude for that airspeed and reduce power at the same time to the setting for that airspeed; if the power comes off in proportion to the pitch change, the airspeed stays constant

body.p: On a PFD, keep climb power until the airspeed nears cruise, watch the altimeter as the speed builds, and use the airspeed trend vector to see how soon the target speed will arrive [[23:209|IFH 7-48]]. The altitude trend vector helps too: start at 10 percent of the vertical speed and keep the trend vector on the target altitude as it shrinks. It is a supplement, not the primary means of setting pitch [[23:160|IFH 6-27]].

**From a climbing turn**, the roll-out has its own lead, half the bank angle [[23:181|IFH 7-20]], and as the bank comes off the vertical lift returns, so the pitch must come down too [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]. The airplane sections of the IFH give no order for the two; its helicopter chapter says the level-off from a climbing or descending turn is the same as from a straight one, and the turn can be stopped first, the level-off made first, or both done together [[23:238|IFH 8-15]]. Application: early in training, end the turn and the climb one after the other rather than both at once; climbing and descending turns already need a faster cross-check to control bank as well as pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

bullets: After the first level-off from a climb, check the attitude indicator and adjust the miniature aircraft for level flight at normal cruise [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].
Keep an accelerated cross-check until positively established in straight-and-level flight [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

callout.text: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can create the inversion illusion of tumbling backwards, and the disoriented pilot may push abruptly into a nose-low attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. A smooth level-off with a proper lead is also a safety item.

check.q: Your student climbs at 800 fpm toward 6,000 feet and starts the level-off at 5,990. What happens, and what lead should she use?
check.a: With too little lead the airplane keeps climbing through the transition and overshoots. Lead by 10 percent of the vertical speed: 80 feet, so start at about 5,920 [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

chunks.title: Entering a constant rate descent, straight and turning

body.p: **An entry into a constant rate straight descent or descending turn.** A descent can be made at many airspeeds and attitudes by reducing power, adding drag and lowering the nose [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. The IFH entry works with or without an attitude indicator: first reduce to the descent airspeed while holding straight-and-level flight, then reduce power further to a predetermined setting, lower the nose at the same time to hold the airspeed, and trim off the pressures [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

For a constant rate descent the entry is the same, but once the VSI stabilizes near the desired rate it is primary for pitch, and the airspeed indicator is primary for power. Pitch and power must be closely coordinated when corrections are made, as in climbs [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

Read Figure 7-30 by its labels, not its caption. The caption says constant airspeed descent, but the labels mark the VSI as primary pitch and the airspeed indicator as primary power, and the IFH cites the figure in its constant rate descent sentence [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:179|IFH Figure 7-30]]. The caption's fix, "airspeed high, reduce power", is constant rate logic: in a constant airspeed descent an airspeed error is fixed with pitch [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

On a PFD: reduce power and let the airplane slow in level flight; near the desired airspeed reduce power to a predetermined value, lowering the nose at the same time or the airspeed keeps falling. For a constant rate descent the VSI tape is primary for pitch and the airspeed tape for power [[23:210|IFH 7-49]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. During the transition only the attitude indicator shows pitch accurately; hold the pitch constant and let the airplane stabilize, trim continuously and scan faster [[23:210|IFH 7-49]].

**Descending turns** combine the descent and turn techniques, with a faster cross-check [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. As the bank comes in, the vertical lift component decreases, so check the altimeter, VSI and attitude indicator for the pitch change needed [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]; hold the airspeed with power. Coordinate the roll-in, since aileron use always produces adverse yaw [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

callout.text: Descent entry: slow first, then power back and nose down together. VSI for pitch, airspeed for power.

check.q: Your student starts a 500 fpm descent from cruise by lowering the nose first and pulling power later; the airspeed jumps 15 knots. What does the IFH entry do differently?
check.a: It slows to the descent airspeed in level flight first, then reduces power to a predetermined setting while lowering the nose to hold the airspeed, and trims [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: The stabilized descent, and where students will use it

body.p: **A stabilized constant rate straight descent or descending turn using the vertical speed indicator.** The VSI is primary for pitch and the airspeed indicator for power [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Holding a specific airspeed in a constant rate descent takes pitch and power working together: any change in pitch directly affects the airspeed, and any change in airspeed directly affects the vertical speed as long as the pitch is held constant [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

body.p: The second and third rows use the trade the IFH teaches for level flight: altitude and airspeed are interchangeable, so when they are off in opposite directions pitch alone may fix both, and when both are off the same way pitch and power are needed [[23:169|IFH 7-8]] [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].
**Where students will use it.** The IFH ties this maneuver to real procedures:

bullets: ILS: set up the proper rate of descent at glideslope interception; then, from the outer marker to the middle marker, adjust pitch to keep the proper rate of descent and power to keep the proper airspeed, while holding the localizer and checking the altimeter [[23:283|IFH 9-40]].

Nonprecision approaches: the vertical descent angle and the groundspeed give a target rate of descent from the rate of descent table in the back of the TPP [[23:42|IFH 1-23]]. FII.VIII.A works the numbers.
PAR: the controller calls the deviation above or below the glidepath, and the pilot adjusts the rate of descent to return to it [[23:290|IFH 9-47]].

ATC descents: without "at pilot's discretion" or a descent restriction, descend at an optimum rate to 1,000 feet above the assigned altitude, then at 500 to 1,500 fpm, and advise ATC if unable to descend at least 500 fpm [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]] [[23:299|IFH 10-8]] [[23:300|IFH 10-9]].

Practice patterns: the IFH circling approach patterns end with a 500 fpm rate descent of 500 feet, then a straight constant airspeed climb with gear and flaps coming up, so Tasks D and E meet in one drill [[23:193|IFH 7-32]].

callout.text: Application: chasing the CDI and glidepath needles is a listed ILS error [[23:285|IFH 9-42]]. A student who already holds a steady rate with pitch and fixes the airspeed with power has less to chase when the needle moves.

check.q: Your student asks why she should practice constant rate descents if an ILS has a glideslope to follow. What do you answer?
check.a: On the ILS the pilot keeps the glidepath by adjusting pitch for the proper rate of descent and power for the proper airspeed, the same split as a constant rate descent [[23:283|IFH 9-40]]. On a nonprecision approach she sets a target rate herself from the VDA and groundspeed [[23:42|IFH 1-23]].

chunks.title: Leveling off from a constant rate descent

body.p: **Level-off from a constant rate straight descent or descending turn.** Start before the target altitude. The lead depends on the rate of descent and the technique, and with too little lead the airplane overshoots unless the technique is rapid [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

head: Level-off at
Round-dial technique
Source
rows: An airspeed higher than descent speed

At 500 fpm, lead by 100 to 150 feet. At the lead point, add power to the level flight cruise setting. The nose tends to rise as the speed increases, so hold forward pressure to keep the rate until about 50 feet above, then smoothly raise the nose to the level attitude for that airspeed
Descent airspeed
Lead by about 50 feet, adjusting the pitch to level flight and adding power at the same time to a setting that holds the airspeed
Then
Trim off the pressures and go back to the normal straight-and-level cross-check

body.p: The glass section gives a different lead: to return to cruise, increase power to cruise before raising the pitch, and start the level-off at 10 percent of the rate of descent, 100 feet at 1,000 fpm. A late start tempts a rapid pitch change; avoid rapid changes that could lead to control problems or spatial disorientation [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Bring the power in early, or the airspeed bleeds below the target as momentum decreases [[23:206|IFH 7-45]].

From a descending turn, the roll-out adds vertical lift as the bank comes off, so lower the pitch as the bank decreases [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]; failing to adjust the pitch as the vertical lift increases on roll-out gives a consistent altitude gain [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Application: near the target altitude that gain is exactly what the level-off does not need, so early in training roll out first or keep the two well apart.

callout.text: Ballooning is the classic error here: the nose pitches up on the level-off because forward pressure was not held as power came in [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

check.q: Descending at 500 fpm to level at cruise speed, your student adds power only 50 feet above the altitude, sinks 40 feet below it and the airspeed sags. What changes?
check.a: For a level-off at an airspeed higher than descent speed at 500 fpm, the IFH leads by 100 to 150 feet, adding cruise power at the lead point and holding forward pressure until about 50 feet above [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Risk: illusions, vertical air and safe practice

body.p: Climbing turns, long descending turns and abrupt level-offs each come with an illusion the IFH names. Teach each hazard by name:

bullets: Climbing turns: uncoordinated turns, especially climbing turns, send misleading signals to the brain, and skids and slips feel like banking or tilting [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. Climbing turns are among the situations where acceleration forces overpower gravity and create false sensations [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].

Descending turns: in a prolonged constant rate turn the pilot feels no turn; noticing the altitude loss, the disoriented pilot may pull back and tighten the spiral, the graveyard spiral [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

Level-offs: an abrupt change from climb to level flight can produce the inversion illusion and a push nose-low; a quick throttle reduction (the somatogravic illusion) can lead a disoriented pilot to pull nose-up toward a stall [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

Vertical air: an updraft can give the elevator illusion of climbing and a push nose-low, a downdraft the reverse [[23:73|IFH 3-6]] [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]. In rough air the VSI swings too; average it, do not chase it [[23:138|IFH 6-5]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].
Head movement: after a long turn, moving the head in a different plane can trigger the coriolis illusion, so build a scan with minimal head movement [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

body.p: Let the student feel it. In the IFH climbing while turning demonstration, a slow, coordinated turn of about 50° of bank with the student's eyes closed usually feels like a climb [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. Never fly these maneuvers at low altitude or without an instructor pilot or appropriate safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]].

bullets: Lookout: simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot in the other control seat [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], and see and avoid applies whenever weather permits, IFR or VFR [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]. Failure to clear the area before and while maneuvering is a typical reason for an unsatisfactory [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]].
Who flies: brief the positive three-step exchange of flight controls before the flight [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

Limits: learners should never be allowed to exceed the flight instructor's limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Application: brief a floor for the descents and an airspeed you will not go below in the climbs, and take over if either is reached.
Errors you simulate: the PTS bars the examiner from simulating any condition that may jeopardize safe flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]. Hold yourself to the same rule.

check.q: Your student levels off sharply from a 1,000 fpm climb in actual IMC and says it felt as if the airplane tumbled backwards. What is it, and what is the danger?
check.a: The inversion illusion, from an abrupt change from climb to level flight; the disoriented pilot may push abruptly nose-low [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Teach a smooth level-off with a 10 percent lead [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

chunks.title: Common errors: power setting, pitch attitude, rate and airspeed

body.p: **Common errors related to constant rate climbs and descents.** For S2 the examiner, acting as your student, flies these on purpose [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]]. The PTS says its listed errors may or may not be found in the references [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]; the IFH error lists for climbs and descents [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]] fit under the PTS headings below.

**Failure to use a proper power setting and pitch attitude.** At any given airspeed the power setting decides whether the airplane levels, climbs or descends [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. Application: so each rate at a given airspeed needs its own power, and with the wrong power, pitch can hold the rate or the airspeed but not both.

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Power settings unknown
Power hunting; rate and airspeed slow to settle
Failure to learn and use proper power settings; without them any change of flightpath takes longer [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
Brief approximate settings for each rate; known settings keep pitch and power corrections to a minimum [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]
Overcontrolling pitch on the entry
Nose comes up too far, the VSI overshoots, then a big correction back
Pitch attitudes for the power settings not yet known; impulse to disturb the attitude before the result is known [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]
Small, smooth pressures, a rapid cross-check and patience while the new rate settles [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
New pitch attitude not held
Nose drifts after a correction; the rate never settles
Pitch allowed to change, so the first correction cannot be validated [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
Hold the new attitude and trim it, then judge it [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
Pushing for low airspeed when power is the cause
Nose goes down; the airspeed comes back but the rate falls off
A low power setting, not a nose-high attitude, caused the low airspeed [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]
Cross-check all relevant instruments before an input; rate right and airspeed low calls for power [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]
Same pitch and power, different rate
A hot or heavy day gives a lower rate than last week
The rate depends on weight and atmospheric conditions [[23:208|IFH 7-47]]
Teach the numbers as starting points; fine-tune on the VSI and airspeed [[23:209|IFH 7-48]]

body.p: **Improper correction of vertical rate and airspeed errors.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Chasing the VSI
Pitch follows every needle swing
Failure to cross-check the VSI against the other pitch instruments [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Change pitch on the attitude indicator, the control instrument, and let the needle settle [[23:212|IFH 7-51]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]
Overcontrolling the rate
VSI more than 200 fpm past the rate wanted
Too much pressure for the correction [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
Relax pressure and let the pitch neutralize [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
One number only
Pitch moved for an airspeed error that power should fix, or the reverse
Failure to cross-check both airspeed and vertical speed before changing pitch or power; a change in one may correct the other [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
Application: have her say both numbers before every correction
Scan not sped up
Errors appear during entries and level-offs
Failure to vary the rate of cross-check during speed, power or attitude changes or climb and descent entries [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
A faster cross-check whenever pitch or power changes [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
Lead not set
Overshoots or undershoots the altitude
Failure to note the rate of climb or descent to set the lead [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
10 percent of the vertical speed [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]
Slow-speed level-off
Airspeed sags or altitude wanders leveling at climb or descent speed
Improper pitch and power coordination from a slow cross-check of airspeed and altimeter [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Pitch and power together, in proportion [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]

callout.text: How to show them (Application): fly one entry with a big, quick pitch change and let the student watch the VSI reverse and lag [[23:166|IFH 7-5]], then fly it with a small, smooth change. Then fix a low airspeed with pitch alone and let her see the rate fall away.

check.q: In a steady 500 fpm climb the airspeed is 5 knots low. Your student lowers the nose only. What error is this, and what was the right fix?
check.a: Failure to cross-check both airspeed and vertical speed before correcting [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]. With the rate correct and the airspeed low, add power and lower the nose slightly to hold the rate [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

chunks.title: Common errors: heading, rate of turn, coordination and trim

body.p: **Improper correction of heading or rate-of-turn errors.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Heading left out
Heading drifts as power comes in for a climb
Failure to cross-check the heading indicator during changes in power or pitch [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Heading in every pass; rudder with the throttle [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]
Too much bank for the correction
A 10° heading error fixed with 20° of bank overshoots
Correcting with improper bank [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Bank no more than the degrees to turn, never more than standard rate [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
Rate of turn off in a climbing or descending turn
Turn coordinator or turn rate trend off the standard rate mark
Overcontrolling and overbanking on entry, or not holding the bank that equals standard rate [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]

Hold the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft on the mark and adjust the bank when it deviates [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]; on a PFD the turn rate indicator is primary [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]
Fixation on one bank instrument
Stares at the turn rate indicator while pitch and rate wander
Abandoning the cross-check [[23:213|IFH 7-52]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
A modified radial scan [[23:213|IFH 7-52]]

body.p: **Uncoordinated use of controls.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Power yaw not countered
Heading swings left as climb power comes in
More power yaws and rolls the airplane left; in a climb, P-factor and torque add to it [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]
Right rudder and aileron with the power; be ready with left rudder as power comes off [[24:80|AFH 3-19]] [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]
Ball ignored in the turn
Turn coordinator on the mark, ball off center
Failure to check the ball; unless it is centered, do not assume the turn comes from bank [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Ball toward the turn: slip, add rudder on that side or reduce bank. Ball away from the turn: skid, relax rudder or add bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]
Slipping climbing turn
Little or no altitude gain in the turn
Improper coordination makes a slip that counteracts the rate of climb [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Coordinated aileron and rudder on the roll-in [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]

body.p: **Improper trim control.**

head: Error
What you see
Usual cause
Fix and how to teach it
rows: Pressures held, not trimmed
Pitch wanders whenever attention goes elsewhere
Failure to trim off pressures: the pilot cannot tell whether a pressure change comes from aerodynamic changes or from his or her own movements [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]
Trim after each change; trim lets the pilot fly without holding pressure and validate a correction [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]
No trim after power changes
Pressure builds after every throttle movement
Failure to trim following power changes [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]; continuous trim changes are needed as the power changes [[23:206|IFH 7-45]]
Trim frequently and in small amounts [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Chasing the VSI blocks trimming
Constant small pitch changes and tension
Overcontrolling leads to tension and prevents sensing the pressures to be trimmed off [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Hold a pitch with pressure, then trim [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]
Trim used to fly
Attitude changed with the trim wheel
Trim used to change pitch instead of relieving pressure; the airplane is trimmed for airspeed, not attitude [[23:206|IFH 7-45]]
Hold the attitude with the yoke first, then trim [[23:206|IFH 7-45]] [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]

callout.text: How to show them (Application): add climb power briskly with your feet flat and let the student watch the heading and ball move, then repeat with right rudder [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. For trim, hold back pressure in a rate climb without trimming, then let go with her watching the VSI.

check.q: In a constant rate descent your student holds back pressure on the yoke and keeps adjusting pitch. What trim error is this, and why does it matter?
check.a: Failure to trim off pressures: unless trimmed, she cannot tell whether a pressure change comes from aerodynamic changes or from her own movements [[23:180|IFH 7-19]], and she cannot validate a correction while holding pressure [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

chunks.title: Building the lesson: sequence, practice and assessment

body.p: When more than one skill is taught at a time, simple to complex works well; when the new skill builds on known ones, known to unknown helps [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Constant rate work builds on straight-and-level flight, airspeed changes and constant airspeed climbs, since the IFH builds the rate climb entry on the constant airspeed entry [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. A sequence that follows the IFH (the order is Application):

head: Step
What the student practices
Source
rows: 1. Straight climbs from climb speed
Slow in level flight, then power and pitch together; airspeed, then VSI, for pitch
2. Straight descents
Slow first, predetermined power, nose down; VSI for pitch, airspeed for power
3. Level-offs
At cruise and at climb or descent airspeed, with the right lead
4. Climbing and descending turns
The straight technique combined with standard rate turns; a faster cross-check
5. Patterns
The circling approach patterns' 500 fpm rate descent and constant airspeed climb, once the basic maneuvers are reasonably good
6. Partial panel
Steps 1 to 5 with the gyros covered or the AHRS simulated

body.p: Then mix them. Blocked practice, the same drill over and over, scores well in the session but gives poorer long-term learning; random practice gives better retention [[25:78|AIH 3-27]]. A student who flies a maneuver well but may not understand it should vary it or combine it with others [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], for example a descending turn that must end on a heading and an altitude.

Assess against standards suited to her stage, looking at her mastery of each element rather than only the overall performance [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. After a scenario, use collaborative assessment: her self-assessment first, then a discussion comparing it with yours [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Application: before the flight, have the student write down the approximate power for 500 fpm up and down at the planned airspeeds, and the level-off leads. It turns the first K2 error, not knowing the power settings, into a preflight item.

check.q: Your student flies straight 500 fpm descents well all morning. How do you check that she understands, not just repeats?
check.a: Have her vary the maneuver or combine it with others [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], such as a descending turn to a heading and altitude, and mix the drills, since random practice gives better retention than blocked practice [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

body.p: In the telling-and-doing technique you **demonstrate and simultaneously explain**: fly while explaining the power settings and attitudes, in the same order you briefed; if the demonstration strays from the explanation, say so at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Next the student tells while you fly, so you can check her understanding before she is busy on the controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. The PTS expects the explanation to be clear, concise, technically accurate and complete with no prompting [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]].
**Constant rate climb, primary-and-supporting words:**

bullets: "Level at climb speed: altimeter primary for pitch, heading indicator for bank, airspeed for power [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]."
"Power up to the setting for 500 feet a minute, and at the same time the nose up to the climb attitude. Right rudder as the power comes in [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]."
"Airspeed is primary for pitch while the VSI settles. I hold this attitude and give the needle a few seconds [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]."
"Needle steady near 500: now the VSI is primary for pitch and the airspeed is primary for power. Trim [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]."
"Rate is good, airspeed two knots low: a little power, and the nose down a hair to keep 500 [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]."
"Fifty feet to go at 500 a minute: forward pressure to the level attitude, keep climb power until we near cruise, then cruise power and trim [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]."

body.p: **Constant rate descent, a turn and the level-off:**

bullets: "Slowing to descent speed in level flight first. Now power back to the setting we planned, nose down to hold the airspeed, trim [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]."
"VSI settling at 500 down: VSI primary for pitch, airspeed primary for power. Airspeed a bit high, so a little less power [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:179|IFH Figure 7-30]]."
"Rolling into a left standard rate turn: nose up slightly to hold 500 as the vertical lift drops, ball centered, turn coordinator on the mark [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]."
"Rolled out. Level-off at cruise speed: 150 feet to go, cruise power in, forward pressure holds 500 down until about 50 feet, then smoothly level and trim [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]."

body.p: **Partial panel version:** "Gyros covered. Pitch from the airspeed indicator, then the VSI once it settles, with small inputs. Bank from the turn coordinator, ball centered. Compass only when we are steady [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]."

The same climb in control-and-performance words: "I set the approximate power for 500 feet a minute on the power gauges and the attitude for that rate and airspeed on the attitude indicator, trim, then cross-check the VSI and airspeed and adjust attitude and power together [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]] [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]."

check.q: During your demonstration the VSI overshoots to 700 fpm while you keep talking about 500. What should you do?
check.a: Acknowledge and explain the deviation at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]], then fix it in words the student can use: a small pitch change on the attitude indicator, then let the needle settle [[23:209|IFH 7-48]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

chunks.title: Analyze and correct: when the examiner flies the errors

body.p: For S2 you **analyze and correct simulated common errors**: the evaluator acts as a student so you can show you recognize, analyze and correct them [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]]. Use the same steps every time: what you see, the name of the error, its cause, the fix, and a short demonstration if asked.

head: Examiner flies
You say
Source
rows: Adds power for a 500 fpm climb and pulls the nose well up at once; the VSI shoots past 1,000 and comes back
"Overcontrolling pitch on the entry. Small, smooth pressure: set the attitude and let it settle."
Holds 500 fpm with the airspeed 8 knots low, then lowers the nose only
"The rate was right, so the airspeed needed power. Add power and lower the nose slightly to keep 500."
Moves the yoke with every VSI swing in light chop
"Chasing the VSI. Average the needle, cross-check the altimeter, and change pitch on the attitude indicator."
Left climbing turn, ball displaced to the left, climb rate falling
"That's a slip, and it's costing climb. Left rudder or a little less bank, and keep the ball centered."
Holds back pressure throughout and never trims
"Trim that pressure off. Until it's trimmed, you can't tell the airplane's changes from your own."
Levels off from a 500 fpm descent and the nose pitches up as power comes in
"Ballooning. Hold forward pressure to keep the rate as the power comes in, then level at about 50 feet."
Starts the level-off from a 1,000 fpm climb at the target altitude
"No lead. Ten percent of the vertical speed: start 100 feet early."

body.p: Correcting is not taking over at the first mistake. Safety permitting, let the student go part way into the error and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; if safety requires it, take the controls with the positive exchange [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

callout.text: Application: when two errors show at once, such as a chased VSI and a low airspeed, name the cause first. Often one fix covers both: hold the attitude, then correct the airspeed with power [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

check.q: In a descending turn the examiner holds the rate on the VSI, but the turn coordinator sits past the standard rate mark with the ball centered. What do you say?
check.a: A rate-of-turn error from too much bank: shallow the bank to put the miniature aircraft back on the mark [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Less bank adds vertical lift, so expect to lower the nose slightly to keep the rate [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

scenario.title: Getting ready for the first ILS: rate climbs and descents, full and partial panel
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII. Your instrument student, a private pilot, flies the school's round-dial, fixed-pitch trainer. Her first ILS lesson is next week, so today is constant rate climbs and descents at 500 fpm, straight and turning, first full panel and then with the attitude and heading indicators covered. It is VMC with 5 miles in haze, the practice area lies under a busy arrival route, and you are the safety pilot.

questions.q: On the ground she asks why she can't fly these like last week's constant airspeed climbs. What is the difference, and why does it matter for the ILS?
questions.a: In a constant airspeed climb, power stays at the climb setting and pitch holds the airspeed; in a constant rate climb, once the needle settles, pitch holds the VSI rate and power holds the airspeed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. On the ILS she will adjust pitch for the proper rate of descent and power for the proper airspeed [[23:283|IFH 9-40]].

questions.q: On her first climb entry she adds full power and pulls the nose well up; the VSI swings past 1,200 fpm and back. Name the error and the fix.
questions.a: Overcontrolling pitch on the climb entry, from not yet knowing the pitch attitudes that go with the power settings [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Set the approximate power for 500 fpm and the climb attitude together, use the airspeed indicator for pitch until the VSI settles [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], and use small, smooth pressures [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

questions.q: In a climbing right turn the ball sits right of center and the climb rate falls to 300 fpm. What do you say?
questions.a: Ball toward the turn means a slip: add right rudder or reduce the bank [[23:89|IFH 4-12]]. A slip from improper coordination counteracts the rate of climb [[24:81|AFH 3-20]], and the bank itself costs vertical lift, so raise the nose slightly and hold the airspeed with power [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

questions.q: You cover the gyros. Descending at 500 fpm, she reaches the level-off altitude still descending and then pulls hard. What do you teach?
questions.a: Start the level-off early: about 50 feet to stay at descent speed, or 100 to 150 feet with power added to level at cruise speed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. With limited instruments, only small, precise inputs; rapid movements compound the deviation and can disorient [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

questions.q: Back in level flight, approach control calls traffic 1,000 feet below you just as she is about to start the next descent. What is your job?
questions.a: Look outside: in simulated instrument flight you are the safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], and see and avoid applies whenever weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]]. Application: hold the descent until the traffic is in sight and clear; failure to clear the area while maneuvering is a typical unsatisfactory on the CFII test [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]].

questions.q: In the debrief she says, "The descents were fine." How do you assess the flight?
questions.a: Collaborative assessment: her self-assessment first, then a discussion comparing it with yours [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], judging each element rather than only the overall performance [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Then plan the circling approach pattern's 500 fpm rate descent as the next step [[23:193|IFH 7-32]].

skills.do: From the right seat, fly a constant rate climb and a constant rate descent, straight and in a standard rate turn, to the instrument pilot skill level, explaining the entry, the primary instruments, the pitch and power corrections and the level-off in your chosen method's words; then repeat with the gyros covered or the AHRS simulated.
skills.practice: Rehearse the talk-through scripts aloud with a safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], demonstrating in the same order you explain and admitting any deviation at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

skills.do: When the examiner, acting as your student, flies a constant rate error, say what you see, name it, give its cause and the fix, and show the fix if asked; take the controls with the positive exchange if safety requires it.
skills.practice: Take turns with another applicant flying the IFH error lists for climbs, descents and turns [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] in VMC, never simulating anything that could jeopardize safe flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]].

quiz.q: Your student asks what changes between a stabilized constant airspeed climb and a stabilized constant rate climb. What do you say?
options: Pitch now holds the VSI rate and power the airspeed
Pitch still holds airspeed; power stays at climb power
Power now holds the rate; the altimeter is primary
Nothing but the target number on the VSI changes
quiz.why: Constant rate: the VSI is primary for pitch once it stabilizes and the airspeed indicator primary for power. Constant airspeed: the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch and the tachometer or manifold pressure gauge for power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. The option that keeps pitch on the airspeed describes Task D.

quiz.q: During the entry to a 500 fpm climb your student watches the VSI swing and keeps changing pitch. Until the rate nears 500, which instrument is primary for pitch?
options: The vertical speed indicator
The altimeter
The airspeed indicator
The manifold pressure gauge
quiz.why: As the power is increased, the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch until the vertical speed approaches the desired value; then the VSI becomes primary for pitch [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

quiz.q: Stabilized at 500 fpm up, the rate is right but the airspeed is 5 knots low. What does the IFH say to do?
options: Lower the nose only and accept less rate
Add power and lower the nose slightly
Raise the nose a little and hold power
Reduce power and hold the same attitude
quiz.why: If the vertical speed is correct but the airspeed is low, add power; as the power increases, lower the miniature aircraft slightly to keep the vertical speed constant [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Lowering the nose alone trades the rate for airspeed.

quiz.q: Your student makes a large, abrupt pitch change to fix a rate error on a round-dial VSI. What will the needle do?
options: Jump at once to the new, accurate rate of climb
Stay still until the altimeter needle starts to move
Lag less than usual, since the change was so large
Move erratically, maybe reverse, settle late
quiz.why: A large and abrupt pitch change produces erratic needle movement, a reverse indication and a greater lag before the needle stabilizes [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

quiz.q: Moving to a glass panel, your student says she will wait 6 to 9 seconds for the VSI tape after each pitch change. What is accurate?
options: No lag on the tape, but the airplane still needs time to settle
The tape lags longer than a round-dial VSI, so wait even more
The tape lags exactly like the round-dial VSI she learned on
The tape is no use for pitch; she should use the altimeter alone
quiz.why: Glass displays use a digital air data computer that does not indicate a lag [[23:197|IFH 7-36]]. Changes still do not produce instantaneous, stabilized results, so patience is needed while the rate settles [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

quiz.q: Climbing at 700 fpm toward 7,000 feet, when should your student start the level-off by the IFH rule of thumb?
options: About 6,993 feet
About 6,650 feet
About 6,930 feet
At 7,000 feet
quiz.why: Lead by 10 percent of the vertical speed: 70 feet at 700 fpm [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. Starting at 7,000 feet means the airplane keeps climbing through the transition.

quiz.q: Descending at 500 fpm on round dials, your student will level off at cruise speed. Where does the IFH add the power?
options: About 50 feet above the altitude
At the altitude, then raise the nose quickly
About 300 to 400 feet above the altitude
About 100 to 150 feet above the altitude
quiz.why: For a level-off at an airspeed higher than descending speed at 500 fpm, lead by 100 to 150 feet and add cruise power at the lead point [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. About 50 feet is the lead for a level-off at descent airspeed.

quiz.q: On the level-off from a descent, your student's nose pitches up and she climbs 80 feet as the power comes in. What is the cause?
options: Too much nose-down trim before the level-off
No forward pressure held as the power came in
VSI lag that hid the climb until it was late
Leading the altitude by 10 percent of the rate
quiz.why: Ballooning comes from failure to maintain the descending attitude with forward pressure as power is increased to the cruise setting [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

quiz.q: With the attitude and heading indicators covered, how does the IFH make climb entries easier to control?
options: Enter from climbing speed
Enter from cruise with full power at once
Hold pitch with the magnetic compass
Trim full nose-up, then add the power
quiz.why: Climb entries on partial panel are more easily and accurately controlled if entering the maneuver from climbing speed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

quiz.q: In a descending left turn the VSI grows from 500 to 650 fpm as your student rolls in, with the airspeed steady. What do you coach?
options: Add power to slow the descent back to 500 fpm
Shallow the bank until the VSI reads 500 again
Raise the nose slightly; the bank cost vertical lift
Wait it out; the VSI is lagging and will settle
quiz.why: As the bank increases, the vertical lift component decreases; check the altimeter, VSI and attitude indicator for the pitch adjustment needed [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. In a constant rate descent pitch holds the rate and power holds the airspeed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]], and the bank sets the rate of turn [[23:88|IFH 4-11]].

quiz.q: This IFH figure is captioned as a constant airspeed descent. Which labels show it is really set up for a constant rate descent?
options: Airspeed primary pitch, tachometer primary power
Altimeter primary pitch, airspeed power
Attitude indicator primary for pitch and bank
VSI primary pitch, airspeed primary power
quiz.why: The labels mark the VSI as primary pitch and the airspeed indicator as primary power [[23:179|IFH Figure 7-30]], the constant rate descent split [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. In a constant airspeed descent an airspeed deviation calls for a pitch adjustment [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

quiz.q: In a constant rate climb your student holds back pressure and never trims. Why does the IFH call this an error?
options: Holding pressure makes the VSI lag much longer than normal
It makes the airspeed indicator read too high
She can't tell her own inputs from aerodynamic changes
Trim matters only for the level-off at the end
quiz.why: Unless the airplane is trimmed, there is difficulty in determining whether control pressure changes are induced by aerodynamic changes or by the pilot's own movements [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

quiz.q: Your student asks how this maneuver relates to the ILS. What does the IFH say the pilot adjusts on the glidepath?
options: Power for the rate of descent, pitch for airspeed
Pitch for the rate of descent, power for airspeed
Trim for the rate of descent, rudder for course
Nothing; the glideslope sets the rate by itself
quiz.why: During the descent from the OM to the MM the pilot holds the localizer, adjusts pitch attitude to maintain the proper rate of descent and adjusts power to maintain proper airspeed [[23:283|IFH 9-40]].

final_quiz.q: Before takeoff your student's VSI shows 100 fpm down on the ramp. What do you tell her?
options: The VSI is inoperative; don't go
Tap it until it reads zero
Fly by the altimeter alone
Use that reading as zero
final_quiz.why: If the VSI indicates anything other than zero before takeoff, that indication can be referenced as the zero mark [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]; if it cannot be adjusted, take the error into account for pitch control [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

final_quiz.q: Ice blocks the static ports during a 500 fpm climb in IMC. What will the VSI show?
options: A steady 500 fpm climb
A continuous zero
A brief climb, then zero
A slowly rising rate
final_quiz.why: A blocked static system produces a continuous zero indication on the VSI and freezes the altimeter [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. A momentary climb is what the VSI shows when the alternate static source is selected [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: In light chop at 500 fpm down, your student's VSI swings between 300 and 700. What do you teach?
options: Use the average and cross-check the altimeter
Correct every swing to hold exactly 500 fpm on the VSI
Raise the nose each time it touches 700 fpm
Ignore the VSI completely until the air is smooth again
final_quiz.why: In turbulence the average of the fluctuations is the correct reading, and the less sensitive altimeter helps [[23:138|IFH 6-5]] [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]; pilots are cautioned not to chase the needle [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

final_quiz.q: Regaining lost altitude at a planned 500 fpm, your student's VSI shows 800 fpm. How does the IFH classify it?
options: Normal lag that will settle
Acceptable under 1,000 fpm
Overcontrolling
Undercontrolling the pitch
final_quiz.why: When the VSI shows an excess of 200 fpm from that desired, overcontrolling is indicated; at a 500 fpm target, more than 700 fpm is overcontrolling [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

final_quiz.q: On the PFD the VSI shows 1,200 fpm up. Using the IFH trend arithmetic, about how far above the present altitude will the trend vector point?
options: About 120 feet
About 200 feet
About 72 feet
About 12 feet
final_quiz.why: 1,200 ÷ 60 = 20 feet per second, times the 6 seconds of the IFH example = 120 feet, the method of Figure 6-37 [[23:159|IFH 6-26]].

final_quiz.q: Which entry into a constant rate descent does the IFH say works with or without an attitude indicator?
options: Lower the nose first, then reduce power once the speed is high
Pull the power to idle and let the nose drop until stable
Trim nose-down until the VSI shows the rate, then set the power to match
Slow to descent speed level, then power back with the nose down
final_quiz.why: First reduce airspeed to the selected descent airspeed in straight-and-level flight, then reduce power to a predetermined setting while lowering the nose to hold the airspeed, and trim; for a constant rate descent the entry is the same [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

final_quiz.q: Your student will level off from a 500 fpm descent and stay at descent airspeed. What does the IFH give?
options: About a 150-foot lead; cruise power, then level
About a 10-foot lead; raise the nose, then power
About a 50-foot lead; pitch and power together
About a 50-foot lead; cut power, then level
final_quiz.why: To level off at descent airspeed, lead by approximately 50 feet, adjusting the pitch to level flight and adding power at the same time to a setting that holds the airspeed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

final_quiz.q: In a 500 fpm climbing turn the rate drops to 350 and the airspeed sags as your student rolls in. What is the fix?
options: Less bank, with the same pitch and power
A little more pitch and a little more power
Lower the nose to get the airspeed back
Wait; the VSI will catch up in seconds
final_quiz.why: As bank increases the vertical lift decreases, so raise the pitch; with the airspeed indicator primary for power, adjust the throttle as drag increases [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. More pitch alone would cost still more airspeed [[23:209|IFH 7-48]].

final_quiz.q: In the IFH glass example the PFD's primary instrumentation fails. Which standby instruments are left?
options: Airspeed, attitude, altimeter, compass
Airspeed, VSI, altimeter, turn coordinator
Attitude, VSI, turn coordinator, compass
Altimeter, VSI, compass, heading indicator
final_quiz.why: The standby instrumentation consists of an analog airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and magnetic compass, and there is no standby turn coordinator [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. None of them is a VSI.

final_quiz.q: ATC clears your student from 8,000 down to 4,000 feet with no pilot's discretion. What rate does the AIM expect in the last 1,000 feet?
options: At least 1,500 fpm
Exactly 500 fpm
Any rate she likes
final_quiz.why: Descend at an optimum rate to 1,000 feet above the assigned altitude, then attempt 500 to 1,500 fpm; advise ATC if unable to descend at least 500 fpm [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]]. Any rate applies only with "at pilot's discretion" [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]].

final_quiz.q: In IFH circling approach pattern I, what follows the 500 fpm rate descent of 500 feet at point E?
options: A level, standard rate turn back to the original entry heading
A straight constant airspeed climb, gear and flaps up
A 500 fpm constant rate climb in a left turn
A level-off and a slowdown to approach speed
final_quiz.why: At E, enter a 500 fpm rate descent; at the end of a 500-foot descent, enter a straight constant-airspeed climb, retracting gear and flaps [[23:193|IFH 7-32]].

final_quiz.q: Your student levels off abruptly from a climb in IMC and feels she is tumbling backward. What is the danger?
options: A sharp pull up into a stall
A roll back into the old turn
An abrupt push into a nose-low attitude
A freeze of her whole cross-check
final_quiz.why: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can create the inversion illusion, and the disoriented pilot may push abruptly into a nose-low attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. A pull toward a stall goes with a quick throttle reduction [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

final_quiz.q: As climb power comes in, your student's heading drifts left. What correction belongs in your explanation?
options: Left rudder to follow the yawing nose
Less power until the heading holds
Rudder trim only, after the climb is set
Right rudder and aileron with the power
final_quiz.why: With an increase in power the airplane tends to yaw and roll left unless aileron and rudder counter it [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]; in a climb, torque and P-factor are countered with right rudder and aileron [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

final_quiz.q: Your student flies straight rate climbs and descents well. Following the AIH and IFH, what do you add next?
options: Climbing and descending turns, then mixed drills
More straight descents until every one is perfect
Partial panel straight climbs only, never turns
Nothing new until her checkride date is booked
final_quiz.why: Simple to complex [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]: climbing and descending turns combine the straight technique with turns [[23:185|IFH 7-24]], and random practice gives better long-term retention than blocked practice [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner, as your student, climbs at 700 fpm with the airspeed 5 knots low, aiming for 500. What fix do you give?
options: Add power and hold the climb attitude
Raise the nose a little to bring the rate back down
Nose down slightly, then see if power is needed
Reduce power and hold the present climb attitude
final_quiz.why: If the vertical speed is high and the airspeed is low, lower the miniature aircraft slightly and note the increase in airspeed to see whether a power change is also necessary [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner chases the VSI in a constant rate descent. Which cause and fix do you name?
options: VSI out of calibration; have it checked and repaired before the next flight
Other pitch instruments not cross-checked; change pitch on the attitude indicator
Too much nose-down trim; roll in nose-up trim until the needle settles
Power set too high; bring it back toward idle and let the rate settle
final_quiz.why: Failure to cross-check the VSI against the other pitch control instruments results in chasing the vertical speed [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]; always use the attitude indicator as the control instrument on which to change the pitch [[23:212|IFH 7-51]].

final_quiz.q: On a hot day at maximum weight, your student's usual pitch and power give 300 fpm instead of 500. What does the IFH say?
options: The VSI has gone out of calibration in the summer heat
The tachometer reads too high in hot weather
The attitude indicator has precessed nose-up today
Rate varies with weight and atmospheric conditions
final_quiz.why: With a smooth pitch transition the VSI stabilizes on a rate equivalent to the pitch and power, and depending on weight and atmospheric conditions this rate will be different [[23:208|IFH 7-47]].

takeaways: Constant airspeed: pitch holds the airspeed, power stays put. Constant rate: pitch holds the VSI rate, power holds the airspeed.
Entry: slow to climb or descent speed first, then power and pitch together; the airspeed indicator leads pitch until the VSI settles.
Rate right and airspeed low: power plus a little nose down. Rate high and airspeed low: nose down first, then check power.
A round-dial VSI shows the trend at once and the rate after a few seconds; abrupt changes make it lag and reverse. Glass VSI tapes have no lag.
Lead level-offs by 10 percent of the vertical speed; from a 500 fpm descent to cruise speed, add power 100 to 150 feet early and hold forward pressure.
In climbing and descending turns the bank costs vertical lift: a little more pitch, power for the airspeed and a faster scan.
Partial panel: enter from climb or descent speed, make small inputs, and fly the bank on the turn coordinator.
An ILS is flown like a constant rate descent: pitch for the rate, power for the airspeed.
cfi_notes: IFH Figure 7-30 is captioned "Constant airspeed descent, airspeed high, reduce power," but its labels make the VSI primary for pitch and the airspeed indicator primary for power, and the IFH cites it in its constant rate descent sentence [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:179|IFH Figure 7-30]]. In a constant airspeed descent an airspeed error is fixed with pitch [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Teach the labels; an examiner may use the figure as a trap.

The level-off leads differ. Round dials: from a 500 fpm descent, 100 to 150 feet when leveling at a higher airspeed and about 50 feet at descent airspeed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Glass: 10 percent of the rate, with power to cruise before the pitch comes up [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]; the trend vector pages and the glass altitude-return text also use 10 percent [[23:160|IFH 6-27]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]], and climbs use 10 percent in both sections [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] [[23:209|IFH 7-48]]. The IFH does not explain the bigger round-dial lead; a likely reason is that power goes in at the lead point while the rate is held until about 50 feet above [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Pick one rule per airplane and say why.

The glass VSI tape shows no lag [[23:197|IFH 7-36]], yet the IFH glass procedure still keeps the airspeed tape primary for pitch until the vertical speed stabilizes [[23:209|IFH 7-48]]. The IFH does not say why; the honest explanation is that the airplane itself needs time to settle at a new rate [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

The IFH text on constant rate maneuvers is short: on round dials, one paragraph on the climb entry and one on corrections [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:177|IFH 7-16]], two sentences for descents [[23:178|IFH 7-17]], and one paragraph for all climbing and descending turns [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]; the glass section adds a few paragraphs on climbs and one on descents [[23:209|IFH 7-48]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Expect to build the turning version yourself from the standard rate turn technique [[23:181|IFH 7-20]], and to say so if asked.

The PTS lists "rate-of-turn errors" [[FAA-S-8081-9E:35|PTS VI.E K2b]], and the IFH has no constant rate list for them; the turn error lists [[23:186|IFH 7-25]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] and the glass standard rate errors [[23:212|IFH 7-51]] [[23:213|IFH 7-52]] supply the content. The PTS itself says its listed errors may or may not be found in the references [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]].

In the IFH glass example the standby instruments are an airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and compass, with no VSI and no turn coordinator [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. A constant rate on standby instruments depends on the airplane's equipment; check its AFM supplement.

IFH 10-9 allows a level-off at 2,500 feet above the airport before a Class B, C or D surface area [[23:300|IFH 10-9]], while the current AIM says Class C or D [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]]. Teach the AIM wording.

Expect the examiner to ask how Task E differs from Task D, which instruments are primary during the entry and once stabilized, the level-off leads, what ballooning is, how partial panel changes the entry, and to fly an error such as fixing a low airspeed with pitch alone. The evaluator acts as a student and expects explanations with no prompting [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:15|PTS Unsatisfactory Performance]].
gaps: No source gives the power settings for a given rate and airspeed in a particular trainer; the IFH says only "the approximate setting for the desired rate" [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]. Get them from the POH/AFM and flight practice.

The CFII PTS gives no tolerances for this Task. The Instrument Rating ACS standard is altitude ±100 feet in level flight, selected headings ±10°, airspeed ±10 knots and bank ±5° during turns [[FAA-S-ACS-8C:16|IR ACS IR.IV.A.S1]] (the Instrument lesson IR.IV.A lists them).

No source gives a separate partial panel procedure for constant rate climbs, descents or rate turns; this lesson applies the IFH partial panel guidance [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:197|IFH 7-36]] and marks that as Application.

No airplane section of the IFH says in what order to roll out and level off from a climbing or descending turn; only the helicopter chapter does, and it allows either order or both together [[23:238|IFH 8-15]]. The advice to separate them early in training is Application.
No source gives a constant rate technique for standby instruments without a VSI, which the IFH glass example lacks [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

activities.title: Task D or Task E?
activities.intro: Tap each statement about the stabilized maneuver, then the maneuver it belongs to, or Both.

items.t: Tachometer or manifold pressure primary for power
Any airspeed error: a small pitch correction
Airspeed low, rate right: add power, nose down slightly
Heading indicator primary for bank when straight
Lead the level-off by 10 percent of the vertical speed

activities.why: Primaries and corrections from [[23:175|IFH 7-14]], [[23:176|IFH Figure 7-27]] and [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]; the 10 percent lead is the IFH level-off rule for climbs [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

activities.title: True or false: the VSI
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A VSI that reads 100 fpm down on the ramp can still be used; that reading becomes zero.
cards.why: True. If the VSI reads other than zero before takeoff, that indication can be referenced as the zero mark [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]; the IFH says to take the error into account [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

cards.s: A big, abrupt pitch change gets the VSI to the new rate faster.
cards.why: False. A large, abrupt change produces erratic needle movement, a reverse indication and a longer lag [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

cards.s: On the IFH glass display, the VSI tape shows altitude changes with no lag.
cards.why: True. The digital air data computer does not indicate a lag [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

cards.s: With the static ports blocked, the VSI keeps showing the climb rate.
cards.why: False. A blocked static system produces a continuous zero on the VSI [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

cards.s: In turbulence, the average of the VSI swings is the reading to use.
cards.why: True. The average of the fluctuations should be considered the correct reading, and the less sensitive altimeter helps [[23:138|IFH 6-5]] [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

cards.s: The airspeed indicator has a built-in lag like the VSI's.
cards.why: False. Its apparent lag comes from the time the airplane takes to accelerate or decelerate; there is no appreciable lag from the instrument itself [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

activities.title: Pitch first, or power?
activities.intro: Tap each picture from a constant rate maneuver, then the fix it needs.
buckets: Pitch first; it may fix both
Power, with a small pitch change

items.t: Climbing: rate 200 fpm high, airspeed 5 knots low
Descending: rate 200 fpm too high, airspeed 5 knots high
Descending: rate 200 fpm too low, airspeed 5 knots low
Climbing: rate on target, airspeed 5 knots low
Climbing: rate 150 fpm low, airspeed on target
Descending: rate on target, airspeed 10 knots high

activities.why: Climb examples from [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] and [[23:209|IFH 7-48]]; Figure 7-30's caption says "airspeed high, reduce power" [[23:179|IFH Figure 7-30]]. When the rate and the airspeed are off in opposite directions, the IFH trade of altitude for airspeed applies and pitch alone may fix both [[23:169|IFH 7-8]] [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. With the rate low and the airspeed right, more pitch alone soon costs airspeed, so power is needed too [[23:209|IFH 7-48]].

activities.title: A constant rate climb from cruise, start to finish
activities.intro: Put the steps in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Reduce to climb speed in straight-and-level flight
Add power to the approximate setting for the rate and raise the nose to the climb attitude together
Hold the attitude with the airspeed indicator primary for pitch while the VSI settles
As the needle stabilizes: VSI primary for pitch, airspeed primary for power; trim
At 10 percent of the vertical speed, ease forward toward the level attitude
Keep climb power until near cruise speed, then set cruise power and trim
activities.why: Entry and primaries from [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]; the lead and the level-off at cruising airspeed from [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

activities.title: Fly circling approach pattern I
activities.intro: Drag each step to the lettered point on the pattern where it happens.

pins.label: Start timing 2 minutes; slow to approach speed
Standard rate turn 45° left, then 45 seconds straight
Turn to the original heading; gear and flaps down
500 fpm rate descent for 500 feet, then a constant airspeed climb

activities.why: Pattern I steps from [[23:193|IFH 7-32]]. The patterns simulate maneuvers met on instrument flights and come after a reasonable degree of proficiency in the basic maneuvers [[23:191|IFH 7-30]].

activities.title: Leads, rates and trends
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Climbing at 800 fpm to an assigned altitude. By the IFH rule, how many feet before the altitude do you start the level-off?
items.why: 10 percent of the vertical speed: 800 × 0.10 = 80 feet [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

items.q: On a PFD the VSI shows 600 fpm down. Using the IFH trend arithmetic (6 seconds ahead), how many feet below the present altitude will the trend vector point?
items.why: 600 ÷ 60 = 10 feet per second, × 6 seconds = 60 feet, the method of Figure 6-37 [[23:159|IFH 6-26]].

items.q: The circling pattern calls for a 500-foot descent at 500 fpm. How many minutes does it take?
items.why: 500 fpm means 500 feet in one minute [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]; the pattern is on [[23:193|IFH 7-32]].

items.q: Your student is 150 feet low. By the IFH rule, what rate of return should she use?
items.why: About double the altitude error: 2 × 150 = 300 fpm [[23:139|IFH 6-6]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

items.q: On that 300 fpm return, above what VSI reading is she overcontrolling?
items.why: More than 200 fpm beyond the desired rate: 300 + 200 = 500 fpm [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

items.q: A climbing turn at 90 knots true airspeed. By the IFH 15 percent rule, about what bank gives standard rate?

activities.title: Name that error
activities.intro: Tap what you see, then the name of the error.

pairs.l: Nose pitches up on the level-off as the power comes in
Pitch follows every swing of the needle
Rate right, airspeed low, nose lowered anyway
pairs.r: Airspeed and VSI not both cross-checked

pairs.l: Overshoots the altitude on every level-off
pairs.r: Lead not set from the rate

pairs.l: Holds pressure and can't tell the airplane's changes from her own
Little climb in a turn with the ball toward the turn

activities.why: Ballooning, chasing, cross-check, lead and trim errors from [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]; ball toward the turn is a slip [[23:89|IFH 4-12]], and a slip counteracts the rate of climb [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

activities.title: A rate descent under the hood, one call at a time
activities.intro: Your instrument student flies the school's round-dial trainer under the hood. It is VMC, you are the safety pilot, and the lesson is a 500 fpm constant rate descent of 1,000 feet, straight and then turning.

steps.s: Before the flight she asks how she will know which power to use for 500 fpm.
options: Brief approximate settings from the POH and practice
Tell her to pull power until the VSI reads 500
Use idle power and hold the rate with the nose
Any power will do; the pitch takes care of it
steps.why: Familiarity with the approximate power settings keeps pitch and power corrections to a minimum [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]; failure to learn and use proper power settings is a listed error [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

steps.s: At cruise she lowers the nose for 500 fpm before touching the throttle, and the airspeed climbs 15 knots.
options: Leave it; the airspeed will settle by itself
Show the IFH entry: slow first, then power and nose
Have her raise the nose until the airspeed recovers
Take the controls and fly the rest of the lesson
steps.why: Reduce to descent airspeed in straight-and-level flight, then reduce power to a predetermined setting while lowering the nose to hold the airspeed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Correction does not mean taking over at the first mistake [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

steps.s: Established at 500 fpm, the rate is right but the airspeed is 8 knots high.
options: Raise the nose to slow down
Lower the nose for more rate
Reduce power; nose up slightly
Add power and hold the attitude
steps.why: With the rate on target, the airspeed is a power fix: Figure 7-30's caption is "airspeed high, reduce power" [[23:179|IFH Figure 7-30]], and pitch and power must be closely coordinated [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

steps.s: She rolls into a left standard rate turn and the VSI shows 650 fpm down with the airspeed steady.
options: Add power to stop the extra descent
Shallow the bank until the VSI reads 500
Raise the nose slightly as vertical lift drops
Wait; the VSI is lagging and will settle
steps.why: As the bank increases the vertical lift component decreases; check the altimeter, VSI and attitude indicator for the needed pitch adjustment [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

steps.s: Rolled out, 150 feet above the level-off altitude, she wants to level at cruise speed.
options: Add cruise power now and hold forward pressure
Wait until 50 feet, then add power and level
Raise the nose now; add power at the altitude
Reduce power further and level at the altitude
steps.why: At 500 fpm, lead by 100 to 150 feet for a level-off at an airspeed higher than descent speed: add power at the lead point and hold forward pressure to keep the rate until about 50 feet above [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

steps.s: As the power comes in, the nose rises and she ends up 60 feet above the altitude.
options: Name it ballooning: forward pressure as power comes in
Call it VSI lag and tell her to wait it out
Have her trim nose-up to hold the new altitude
Pull the power back and start the level-off again
steps.why: Ballooning: failure to maintain the descending attitude with forward pressure as power is increased to the cruise setting [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].
